This project represents a completed baseball batting training program built in Unity.

The main structure of the program can be described as four systems running in parallel: 
- the player input system
- the pitch generation system
- the baseball force simulation system
- the bat collision detection system. 

These four systems run continuously throughout the program’s operation and continuously pass relevant output data to each other that is then interpreted uniquely by each system in order for them to successfully fulfill their purposes. The player input system continually gathers sensory input data from the virtual reality apparatus, which is used to update the position and rotation of the player camera and the virtual baseball bat. The player input system also continually outputs relevant position data to be continuously interpreted by the bat collision system. In parallel, the pitch generation system manages a timer and generates a new baseball pitch with unique parameters once that timer reaches zero. The pitch generation system repeats this process continuously and passes on the pitch parameter data to the baseball force simulation system with each pitch generation. Once a pitch has been generated, the baseball force simulation system uses those pitch parameters to continuously simulate the magnus effect and other relevant forces throughout the lifetime of the ball’s trajectory until it collides with an object. It is this relationship between inputs and outputs of these continuous systems that define the general process of this program.

The training program implements physical forces that are not typically accounted for in Unity. 

For example, rotational forces and forces generated by differences in air pressure that play a key role in defining the curved trajectory of baseballs as they fly through the air were not normally taken into consideration in Unity’s default simulation. As a result, to solve this problem, I had to determine how to integrate new force calculations into the already existing Unity system in order to produce different baseball pitches that had not only realistic behaviors, but that could also be thrown for strikes.

Above is a demo of the custom controller designed to be used with the Virtual Reality headset.

The controller sends sensory data from a 9 degree of freedom sensor back to the simulation, where it is then processed to articulate the virtual baseball bat in the simulation.

Using this controller, the player gets the realistic feel of holding a baseball bat, further enhancing the accuracy of the training simulation.

Future developments of this training program could include the following enhancements:

1. Implementing motion capture data for the pitcher for more accurate pitch telegraphing.
2. Implementing a PBR rendering workflow, using realistic custom Unity materials to give depth to the scene.
3. Implementing a custom shader for realistic field grass, made in either Unity HLSL or Unity's Shader Graph.

This is a prototype boat simulator made in unity.

The boat is driven by physically accurate force calculations for airfoils moving through fluids like air or water. This is achieved by calculating the lift and drag forces for each airfoil on the boat: the sail, centerboard, and rudder.
The directions of these forces are either parallel to the fluid velocity (drag) or perpendicular to it (lift).

The magnitudes of these forces are calculated using the lift or drag formula. The magnitudes vary directly by the area of the airfoil and the coefficient of lift or drag, which is a function of angle of attack.

The magnitudes also vary directly by the properties of the fluid they travel in. The sail varies by the density and velocity of the apparent wind, while the centerboard forces are affected by different values set for the ocean's density and realtime apparent velocity.

The functions for the lift and drag coefficients of the airfoils are taken from empirical data, and approximated using piecewise functions to return an accurate coefficient for the state of the boat's airfoils at any direction relative to the fluid direction.

EMPATH is a narrative-based VR action game. The player uses gesture controls to conjure spells from arcane gauntlets which they wield on both arms.

The game was developed as a vertical slice at USC Games.

I was responsible for designing the main character’s assets (first person arms and gauntlets) and the model for the final boss of the game. I also did animation integration in Unreal Engine and made some additional prop art, though the environments were mostly acquired assets due to a lack of 3D artists on the team (I was the only one).

I recreated the classic Frogger game in Unity. I set the game to display at a wonderfully low resolution, and recreated the effect of “pixel-perfect” snapping when sprites move in the scene.

I downloaded and used all the original sprites and audio for the game, and mimicked the functionality of the first level: 3 lives, and 5 goals at the other side of the obstacles.

Hyperspace drifter is an original game made in Unity 1 night.

"Hyperspace is the bridge between worlds. Unknown dangers await. Survive to escape... the Hyperspace Rift!"

Infinidungeon is an early project I made in 8 days to challenge myself.

I made all the textures, models, code... everything except the background music. Admittedly, the audio is the most lacking part.

The player spawns on the outskirts of an ominous dungeon. When they enter, there is no turning back.

The player must kill all the enemies in the current room to move on to the next one. The rooms go on forever as enemies get harder and more in number. The idea is to get the highest score you can before dying!

The name Infinidungeon was inspired by the name of Infiniminer. The idea was to create infinite adventure rather than infinite survival!

The full vision includes expanding rooms and hallways, loot, enemy variety, and... multiplayer?

Infinite Procedural Voxel Terrain.

(Bitshift, I probably don’t have to explain this one to you guys.)

I used 2D perlin noise and 2D chunking for this system.

I implemented chunking, mesh face optimization, and chunk streaming with Unity jobs system.

I wrote the code using C++ native data structures in C# wrappers. This allowed me to invoke the burst compiler, which heavily optimizes the machine code output.

Between the burst compiler and the Jobs system, the chunks load extremely fast!

I got enough satisfaction from this project by getting it to the state you currently see it. My goal was not to recreate Minecraft or make a voxel game— I just wanted to implement an infinite voxel world in my own way.

Next steps would be adding trees by streaming neighboring chunk data to fix chunk seam issues and setting a water height level. That would add some nice features to the landscape!

I built a raytracer in JavaScript, integrated in an Electron environment with Vite (hi Bitshift!). I made this project to gain implementation experience with raytracers from the ground up while also priming my JavaScript skills.

I implemented matrices, vectors, points, rays, and all the associated math functions between them from scratch.

I implemented sphere rendering for now using sphere intersection calculations.

I then implemented the main render function, which follows a phong lighting model.

The renderer is currently offline, but I’m excited at the idea of GPU accelerating it with WebGPU just for fun! I already wrote all the data structures to use performant data types, and it’s quite fun having a JS renderer running as its own Electron app!

Dear Bitshift and Notch— I hope you like it, even though I know it’s still simple. I built it in a week in order to add to my portfolio for you. It was really fun and I can build anything!

I made all the pixel art and animations for the main character and coded the game.

I had some team members make the art for the environment and the art for the cult enemies.

The end credits list way more people than who actually worked on it, as it was a school project with many "non-contributors." It was just me and two other artists as mentioned above.

Original art, animations, and code. Developed in Unity.

Inspired by the third person combat of Dark Souls.

Integrates third-person camera with a third-person melee conbat system. The system gives the player a light attack and a heavy attack mode. There are two animations for each mode that seamlessly blend with each other. Heavy and light attacks and also blend together in a combo. 

Each attack has an "active frame" attack window using unity Animation Event toggles. This gives each attack the structure of "wind-up," "attack," and "recovery." During "wind-up," the player's direction is controllable with both keyboard and mouse, creating a responsive and natural game feel.

The player is also equipped with a sprint and dodge roll.

See video for a full demo.

I created this asset for a game called Turtle Town, but it did not get used due to team dysfunction.

I sculpted and retopologized the turtle model in ZBrush, painted the textures in Substance Painter, and rigged it in Maya LT.

The screenshots you see are in Unity engine with orthographic projection, as was the intended display format for the game project.

The turtle is rendered using a stylized shader which gives an outline effect as well as quantized lighting bands. The shader was part of my art direction, but I did not code it.

The game's focus was to build a base on the back of a giant, living turtle. On the back of the turtle are stylized trees and monolithic rocks that jut from its shell.

The turtle is rigged to animate 3 tiers of progress for the player. Each town hall upgrade clears rocks and trees from the back of the turtle, openning up new areas for the player to expand their city:

The Witch List is a real-time multiplayer PvP spell casting mobile game! Players engage in exciting 1v1 online combat, casting spells with touch gestures and drawing of rune symbols. This project was made as a vertical slice demo at USC Games, and was published on the App Store (no longer available).

I was responsible for designing and creating the characters and the primary combat arena featured in the game.

I used Zbrush and Maya to 3D model the trees, runic arcane bench, bushes and shrubbery. I used ZBrush and Maya to sculpt and topologize the main character’s faces, eyes, and male character body.

For texturing, I used Substance Painter and Maya.

I fully integrated all the assets into Unity, and designed the final game map in-engine.

The shipped game featured some graphical downgrades in order to be compatible with weaker android phones.

This is a prototype for a procedural world generator that generates discrete sized worlds.

The intended use was for generating a tile-based world for a 2D top-down survival game.
Refine world resolution, size, and "feel" with auto-updating perlin noise settings.
Perlin clamping levels can be adjusted to modify the water level, beach size, and overall landmass size.

Voronoi noise is used to generate a biome map. Biomes can be added on the fly. Voronoi settings can be modified to change the number / size of biome groups, as well as the distance function used to classify a cell's biome. Traditional distance gives straight, harsh cutoffs, while Minkowski's distance formula yields cool twisty borders between biomes.
Biomes can also be created in a serialized generation profile. Profiles can be swapped on the fly to generate worlds or levels of different varieties.
